## LoRA {#H01 .lora-slide .opening-chapter background-color="#0a0a0a"}

:::::: {.lora-body .opening-hero}

::: {.opening-hero-copy}
Low-Rank Adaptation

$$
W'=W_0+sBA
$$

Freeze $W_0$ and train $A,B$. The multiplier $s$ is $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/r$ for LoRA and $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/\sqrt{r}$ for rsLoRA. When merging, $\lambda_t$ weights the update for task $t$.
:::

:::: {.opening-factorization}
```{=html}
<div class="opening-matrix-art" role="img" aria-label="A tall thin matrix B times a short wide matrix A produces a full-size matrix BA. Multiplying by the scale s gives the update Delta W. The inner dimension r limits the rank.">
  <span class="opening-matrix opening-matrix-b"><b>B</b></span>
  <span class="opening-matrix-op" aria-hidden="true">×</span>
  <span class="opening-matrix opening-matrix-a"><b>A</b></span>
  <span class="opening-matrix-op" aria-hidden="true">=</span>
  <span class="opening-matrix opening-matrix-product"><b>BA</b></span>
</div>
```

$$
s\,\underbrace{B}_{d_{\rm out}\times r}\quad
\underbrace{A}_{r\times d_{\rm in}}
=\underbrace{\Delta W}_{d_{\rm out}\times d_{\rm in}}
$$
::::

::::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
The update $\Delta W=sBA$ has rank at most $r$. How much freedom does a task need?
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Hu et al. · LoRA · §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685v2#page=4) · [Kalajdzievski · rsLoRA · §3](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.03732v1#S3)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
The adapted layer maps $x$ to $W'x=W_0x+sB(Ax)$. The rank bound applies to the task update because every output change belongs to the column span of $B$. Here $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}$ is a scaling hyperparameter and $s$ is the complete multiplier. Later, $\lambda_t$ weights the already-scaled update from task $t$ when merging. Whether rank $r$ suffices for a task is an empirical question.
:::

### V projection · GPT-3 block 48 of 96
**Rows $i$** and **columns $j$** count leading right singular vectors of the rank-8 and rank-64 $A$ factors, respectively.

$$
\phi(i,j)=\frac{\lVert U_{8,i}^\top U_{64,j}\rVert_F^2}{\min(i,j)}
$$

The outlined $(1,1)$ cell gives the squared cosine between the two leading directions, about 0.43 on the color scale. Gray cells are omitted.

The crop shows the original V zoom from Figure 3. $U_{8,i}$ and $U_{64,j}$ contain the first $i$ and $j$ right singular vectors as orthonormal columns. The diagonal goes from about 0.43 to 0.15 by the plotted color scale. The paragraph below Figure 3 describes the leading similarity as greater than 0.5, which disagrees with the displayed V panel. The slide follows the figure. A score of one means the smaller space is contained in the larger one; zero means they are orthogonal. The figure compares the input subspaces of the learned $A$ factors, so it does not establish that a direction is necessary for the task. The spectrum of a realized weight update comes up on [L50](#/L50).

## Initialize the two factors asymmetrically {#L01 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-mechanism}

::: {.lora-figure .opening-paper data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/paper-l01-hu-fig1.png" alt="Hu et al. Figure 1, showing a frozen pretrained branch in blue and the parallel adaptation branch with a Gaussian A and zero B.">
:::

:::: {.opening-reading}
### Gaussian $A_0$, zero $B_0$

For $W'=W_0+sBA$, the initial update is zero. Write $G=\nabla_{W'}\mathcal L$ for the dense weight gradient.

::: {.opening-ledger}
| Factor | Gradient at initialization |
|:--|:--|
| $A$ | $sB_0^\top G=0$ |
| $B$ | $sGA_0^\top$, generally nonzero |
:::
::::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
The layer starts at the pretrained function. The first loss gradient can move $B$, while $A$ has zero loss gradient.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Hu et al. · LoRA · Fig. 1 and §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685v2#page=1) · [Chen et al. · Learning Rate Scaling · §3.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.06204v1#S3.SS1)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
Starting from $W'=W_0+sBA$, apply the chain rule to get the two displayed gradients. The gradient of $B$ can also vanish if $GA_0^\top=0$. An optimizer with weight decay can move $A$ even when its loss gradient vanishes. We use plain gradient descent when discussing a first step.
:::

## Both factors at zero means neither can move {#L27 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-gradient-flow}

::: {.opening-reading}
### The loss wants a larger weight

For $w=ba$ and $\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12(w-2)^2$, the dense slope at $w=0$ is **$g_w=-2$**. Each factor receives that slope through the other factor.

The paths show the first step at SGD rate $1/4$.
:::

:::: {.opening-flow-diagram}
::: {.opening-flow-row}
**Both factors start at zero**

```{=html}
<div class="opening-flow-edge">
  <span>dense slope −2</span><span>× a₀ = 0</span><strong>∂ℒ/∂b = 0</strong>
</div>
<div class="opening-flow-edge">
  <span>dense slope −2</span><span>× b₀ = 0</span><strong>∂ℒ/∂a = 0</strong>
</div>
```

$w_1=0$ · loss stays at **2**.
:::

::: {.opening-flow-row}
**Only $b$ starts at zero**

```{=html}
<div class="opening-flow-edge opening-flow-active">
  <span>dense slope −2</span><span>× a₀ = 1</span><strong>∂ℒ/∂b = −2</strong>
</div>
<div class="opening-flow-edge">
  <span>dense slope −2</span><span>× b₀ = 0</span><strong>∂ℒ/∂a = 0</strong>
</div>
```

$w_1=0.5$ · loss falls to **1.125**.
:::
::::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
Both starts give $w_0=0$. The nonzero $a_0$ lets the first gradient reach $b$.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Mu and Klabjan · arXiv v1 · Eq. (7) and §4](https://arxiv.org/html/2512.18248v1#S3.SS2) · constructed scalar example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
The scalar partial gradients are $(w-2)b$ and $(w-2)a$. At the origin of the factors they vanish even though the dense derivative $\partial_w\mathcal L=-2$. In the paper, the same phenomenon follows by writing the product via a stacked matrix $V$ and observing that Eq. (7) has a rightmost factor of $V$. For the live start the new loss is $(0.5-2)^2/2=1.125$.
:::

## Keep the initial function when both factors are nonzero {#L02 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-compensation-visual}

::: {.opening-setup}
Set $C=sB_0A_0$ with both factors nonzero. Track entry $(1,2)$ before and after moving $C$ into the adapter.
:::

::: {.lora-figure .opening-wide-figure data-lora-fit="true"}
```{=html}
<picture>
  <source media="(max-width: 650px)" srcset="assets/lora_research_short/01/feedback-l02-mobile.svg">
  <img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/feedback-l02.svg" alt="A worked example splits the original 2 by 2 matrix into a frozen residual and a rank-one adapter contribution. The top-right entry is 2 in the original, 3 in the frozen residual, and minus 1 in the adapter. Their sum is the original matrix.">
</picture>
```
:::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
LoRA-GA subtracts the initial adapter before freezing the residual. Adding it back restores the original forward map at initialization.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Wang et al. · LoRA-GA · §3.4, Algorithm 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/62c4718cc334f6a0a62fb81c4a2095a1-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=6) · constructed entry example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
Algorithm 1 freezes $W_{\mathrm{res}}=W_0-sB_0A_0$. During training, $W'=W_{\mathrm{res}}+sBA$, so its effective change from the checkpoint is $s(BA-B_0A_0)$. This is exact in real arithmetic for a linear branch with adapter dropout inactive. The frozen parameter tensor now holds a residual. As the factors learn, their product changes and adds to that fixed residual.
:::

## PiSSA starts from the weight’s leading singular components {#L03 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-mechanism}

:::: {.opening-reading}
### PiSSA decomposes the pretrained weight $W_0$

At $s=1$ and $r=1$, if $W_0=\operatorname{diag}(9,4)$, train the factors for the leading component and freeze the rest.

$$
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3\\0\end{bmatrix}}_{B_0}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}3&0\end{bmatrix}}_{A_0}
+\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}0&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{frozen}}
=\begin{bmatrix}9&0\\0&4\end{bmatrix}
$$
::::

::: {.lora-figure .opening-paper data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/l03-pissa-ba.svg" alt="The input x goes through A and then B. The parallel frozen residual is added to this output. A and B are initialized with the leading singular vectors and the square roots of the retained singular values.">
:::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
Both branches initially sum to $W_0$. Fine-tuning changes the factors while the residual stays frozen.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Meng et al. · PiSSA · Fig. 1(c)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.02948v4#page=2) · [§3, Eqs. (2)–(5)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.02948v4#page=4) · diagram adapted to column-vector notation
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
Transposing the source’s row-vector convention gives this diagram. For the column-vector weight $W_0=U\Sigma V^\top$, put $B_0=U_r\Sigma_r^{1/2}$ and $A_0=\Sigma_r^{1/2}V_r^\top$ at unit scale. The truncated SVD gives a closest rank-at-most-$r$ approximation in Frobenius norm. Here the original matrix is diagonal with positive entries, so the coordinate directions are its singular directions. Both factors can change during fine-tuning. See [L104](#/L104) for deployment implications.
:::

## LoRA-GA initializes both factors from the gradient {#L10 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

:::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-direction-layout}

::: {.opening-reading}
### LoRA-GA decomposes the dense gradient $G$

Use the same batch for calibration and the first SGD step. Take $G=\operatorname{diag}(6,2)$, $r=1$ and unit factor scales.

1. Put the **first right direction** in $A_0$. Its projector selects the first column of $G$.
2. Put the **second left direction** in $B_0$. Its projector selects the second row of $G$.
:::

:::: {.opening-axis-exhibit}
::: {.lora-figure .opening-axis-figure data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/l10-axis-split.svg" alt="In the singular-vector coordinates of the diagonal gradient, a shaded vertical band selects the first column and a shaded horizontal band selects the second row. The retained entries 6 and 2 occupy different diagonal positions; their first-order sum has rank two.">
:::

The retained entries $6$ and $2$ occupy different diagonal positions. Scale the resulting matrix by $-\eta s^2$ for the first-order step.
::::

::::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
Each $BA$ has rank at most $r$. With compensation, the effective step $s(B_1A_1-B_0A_0)$ can reach rank $2r$.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Wang et al. · LoRA-GA · §3.2, Theorem 3.1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/62c4718cc334f6a0a62fb81c4a2095a1-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=5) · [Algorithm 1](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/62c4718cc334f6a0a62fb81c4a2095a1-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=6) · constructed rank-one example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
Here $A_0=[1,0]$ and $B_0=[0,1]^\top$. With adapter multiplier $s$ and plain SGD rate $\eta$, the first-order effective weight change is $-\eta s^2(GA_0^\top A_0+B_0B_0^\top G)$. The product expansion also includes $s\,\delta B\delta A$, which is second order in the SGD rate. In this example the exact step is upper triangular, with diagonal $-6\eta s^2,-2\eta s^2$ and upper-right entry $12\eta^2s^3$. It has rank two whenever $\eta s\ne0$. Algorithm 1 takes the first $r$ right and next $r$ left singular directions of the dense gradient with a common scaling; its recipe requires $2r\le\min(d_{\rm in},d_{\rm out})$.
:::

:::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-calibration}

:::: {.opening-reading}
### Llama 2-7B · MetaMathQA subset
A **2,048-example** batch serves as the gradient reference. Smaller batches estimate the starting direction.

The agreement metrics compare gradients at initialization. GSM8K accuracy tests the model after fine-tuning.
::::

:::: {.opening-calibration-grid}
::: {.opening-ledger}
| Batch | Sign match | Magnitude match | GSM8K |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 8 | 74.3% | 87.8% | 52.79% |
| 16 | 79.0% | 90.8% | 52.99% |
| 32 | 83.8% | 93.3% | 52.91% |
| 64 | 87.5% | 95.0% | **53.56%** |
| 128 | 90.3% | 96.2% | 52.57% |
| 256 | **92.5%** | **97.1%** | 53.22% |
:::
::::

::::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
Batch 256 agreed best with the reference gradient. Batch 64 scored highest on GSM8K in this sweep.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Wang et al. · LoRA-GA · NeurIPS 2024 §4.6, Table 7](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2024/file/62c4718cc334f6a0a62fb81c4a2095a1-Paper-Conference.pdf#page=10)
:::

Sign match is the fraction of gradient entries sharing a sign. Magnitude match is the fraction whose absolute values are within a factor of ten. The published table reports both similarities as fractions. The slide expresses them as percentages. The 0.34 percentage-point GSM8K difference between batches 64 and 256 is descriptive. Table 7 gives no uncertainty for this comparison. The batch of 2,048 is a reference, not the full-dataset gradient. LoRA-GA uses a backward pass on the calibration examples to estimate this layer’s dense gradient.
:::

## The adapter scale acts twice on the first SGD step {#L14 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

:::::: {.lora-body .opening-case}

::: {.opening-setup}
**Analytical example for SGD.** Start with $B_0=0$ and $W'=W_0+sBA$. Let $G=\nabla_{W'}\mathcal L$ at initialization and use learning rate $\eta$.
:::

::::: {.opening-case-pair}
::: {.opening-case-lane}
### Backward through the adapter

$$
\nabla_B\mathcal L=sGA_0^\top
$$

The gradient of $B$ picks up one $s$. The step leaves $A$ fixed.
:::

::: {.opening-case-lane .opening-live}
### Forward with the new factors

$$
\delta W=-\eta\,s\,(sGA_0^\top)A_0
$$

The outer $s$ comes from the forward map. The inner $s$ came from the gradient.
:::
:::::

::: {.opening-entry}
With the same gradient and initialization, doubling $s$ makes the first weight step **four times as large**.
:::

::::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
The first effective weight step scales quadratically with the adapter multiplier under plain SGD.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Kalajdzievski · rsLoRA · Appendix A Eqs. (6), (8)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.03732v1#page=8)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
At initialization, the pretrained forward map means $G$ is unchanged by $s$ under the assumptions. The first step has $A_1=A_0$ and $B_1=-\eta sGA_0^\top$. These give the exact displayed first-step formula. The paper then studies the dependence on rank under its initialization assumptions. AdamW uses a different update rule.
:::

## rsLoRA kept initial gradient norms aligned across ranks {#L15 .lora-slide .lora-evidence .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-wide-plot}

::: {.lora-figure .opening-paper data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/paper-l15-rslora-fig3.png" alt="Original rsLoRA Figure 3. Average parameter gradient norms measured over training steps for ranks 4 to 2048. LoRA curves begin in widely separated bands; rsLoRA curves begin at similar levels.">
:::

:::: {.opening-reading}
### AdamW experiment · Llama 2 on OpenOrca

| Adapter | Multiplier $s$ |
|:--|--:|
| LoRA | $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/r$ |
| rsLoRA | $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/\sqrt{r}$ |

The chart tracks average **parameter-gradient norms** on a log scale past training step 600, for ranks 4 to 2,048.
::::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
LoRA’s initial gradient norm dropped as rank increased in this run. The rsLoRA curves started at similar levels.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Kalajdzievski · rsLoRA · §3, §4 Fig. 3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.03732v1#page=5)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
This is the authors’ empirical AdamW experiment. The earlier first-step derivation uses plain SGD in effective weight space. Under centered, independent initialization with fixed entry variance, $\mathbb E[A_0^\top A_0]$ is proportional to $rI$, so the leading mean step coefficient is proportional to $rs^2$ (Appendix A, Eq. 9). This motivates comparing $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/r$ and $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}}/\sqrt{r}$.
:::

## LoRA+ gives the two factors separate learning rates {#L17 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-rate-directions}

::: {.lora-figure .opening-rate-figure data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/l17-output-directions.svg" alt="Three output arrows in a two-dimensional coordinate plane. The starting output is at 1,1. Changing A alone extends it in the same direction to 2,2. Changing B alone gives the longer horizontal output 2,0.">
:::

::: {.opening-reading}
### Rank-one adapter · $BAx$

$A$ projects the input into $r$ dimensions. $B$ maps those coordinates into the output space. Here $Ax=1$ and $B=(1,1)^\top$.

**Step in $A$ at rate $\eta_A$.** Doubling $Ax$ stretches the output along the same line.

**Step in $B$ at rate $\eta_B$.** Changing $B$ to $(2,0)^\top$ changes both direction and length.
:::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
LoRA+ gives the two updates different rates. The authors choose a ratio $\eta_B/\eta_A$ and tune the overall rate.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Hayou, Ghosh and Yu · LoRA+ · §§4, 5.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.12354v2#S4) · constructed feature example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
The three arrow endpoints isolate the two effects through illustrative perturbations. The changes are chosen for geometric clarity and do not come from a particular loss gradient. The two first-order feature-change terms in §4 hold either factor fixed. The exact feature change also includes their interaction. The authors’ infinite-width analysis assumes an isolated layer with a fixed input and a suitably processed gradient. In the experiments, the best rate ratio depends on the task and model.
:::

## Unequal rates added 1.3 points on MMLU {#L18 .lora-slide .lora-evidence .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split .opening-heatmap}

::: {.lora-figure .opening-paper data-lora-fit="true"}

## The same product can lead to a different SGD step {#L23 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

:::::: {.lora-body .opening-gauge}

::: {.opening-setup}
For any invertible $r\times r$ matrix $R$, **$BA=(BR)(R^{-1}A)$**.

In one dimension, start with $w=ba=1$, dense slope $-1$ and SGD rate $0.01$.
:::

::::: {.opening-gauge-grid}
::: {.opening-gauge-data .opening-ledger}
### Different factor gradients

| Start $(a,b)$ | Step $\delta a=0.01b$ | Step $\delta b=0.01a$ |
|:--|--:|--:|
| $(1,1)$ | $+0.01$ | $+0.01$ |
| $(10,0.1)$ | $+0.001$ | **$+0.1$** |
:::

:::: {.opening-gauge-result}
### Effective weight after one step

<div class="lora-figure opening-gauge-figure" data-lora-fit="true">
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/l23-product-steps.svg" alt="Two tracks on the same linear product axis start at w equals 1. The balanced start moves a short distance to 1.0201, while the rescaled start moves to 2.0002.">
</div>
::::
:::::

::::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
How does parameterization affect optimization?
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Yen et al. · LoRA-RITE · §§2.1–2.2, Eqs. (5)–(6)](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.20625v2#S2.SS2) · constructed scalar example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
For $\mathcal L(w)=\tfrac12(w-2)^2$, the slope is $-1$ at $w_0=1$. The simultaneous increments in $(a,b)$ are $(0.01b,0.01a)$. The two new products are $1.01^2=1.0201$ and $10.001\times0.2=2.0002$. In the matrix case $A$ represents hidden coordinates whose basis can change via $R$. LoRA-RITE asks whether the optimizer induces the same weight update under such a reparameterization. [DoRA](#/L201) asks a different question about parameterizing a weight vector by its magnitude and direction.
:::

## DoRA learns each weight vector’s length and direction {#L201 .lora-slide .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split}

::: {.lora-figure .opening-rate-figure data-lora-fit="true"}
<img src="assets/lora_research_short/01/l201-dora-column.svg" alt="One pretrained weight column has length 3 and points horizontally. Rotating it keeps length 3. Increasing its learned magnitude to 5 moves its tip farther along the new direction.">
:::

::: {.opening-reading}
### Normalize each column in the paper’s layout

$$
W'=m\odot\frac{W_0+sBA}{\lVert W_0+sBA\rVert_c}
$$

$\lVert V\rVert_c$ gives one Euclidean norm per column. PEFT stores an `nn.Linear` weight transposed and normalizes each output row.

**Train** $m,A,B$. **Freeze** $W_0$. Initialize $m_j$ to the norm of pretrained column $j$ and $B$ to zero.
:::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
The directional correction $sBA$ has rank at most $r$. Column rescaling can make $\operatorname{rank}(W'-W_0)>r$.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Liu et al. · DoRA · Fig. 1, §3.2 and Eq. (5)](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.09353v5#S4.SS1) · [PEFT v0.21.0 · normalization axis](https://github.com/huggingface/peft/blob/v0.21.0/src/peft/tuners/lora/dora.py#L85-L91) · constructed vector example
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
Start at $(3,0)$ and follow the dashed arc to the open circle at $(1.8,2.4)$. Both points have length 3. Continue along the green ray to $(3,4)$. The direction stays $(3/5,4/5)$ as the magnitude grows to 5. In the paper’s convention, $\lVert V\rVert_c[j]=(\sum_i V_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. For an out-by-in PyTorch linear weight, the displayed matrix corresponds to its transpose. PEFT takes the norm over the input dimension, yielding one magnitude per output. With unrestricted scalar parameters the length is $|m_j|$. To see the rank distinction, take $r=1$, $W_0=I_2$, $BA=0$ and $m=(2,2)$. Then $W'-W_0=I_2$ has rank two.
:::

## What does DoRA cost? {#L202 .lora-slide .lora-evidence .opening-chapter}

::::: {.lora-body .opening-split}

::: {.opening-ledger data-lora-fit="true"}
### Supplementary · one adapted layer

| | LoRA | DoRA |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Trainable weights | $A,B$ | $A,B$ + one $m_j$ per output |
| Weight-vector norms | None | Recompute each training forward pass |
| Training work | Low-rank branch | Branch + norms and rescaling |
| Fold for inference | Store $W_0+sBA$ | Store normalized, rescaled $W'$ |
:::

::: {.opening-reading}
### LLaMA-7B · 8 commonsense tasks

| Mean accuracy | LoRA | DoRA |
|:--|--:|--:|
| Rank 32 | 74.7% | **78.4%** |

The authors detach the norm denominator from the gradient graph. It still updates on each forward pass.
:::

:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
DoRA spends extra work on column norms during training. Both methods can serve a single folded weight matrix.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Liu et al. · DoRA · §4.3](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.09353v5#S4.SS3) · [Table 1](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.09353v5#S5.T1) · [Appendix A.2, Table 7](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.09353v5#A1.T7) · [PEFT v0.21.0 · linear weights](https://github.com/huggingface/peft/blob/v0.21.0/src/peft/tuners/lora/dora.py#L140-L153)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
For a $d\times k$ matrix in the paper’s column convention, LoRA trains $r(d+k)$ weights and DoRA trains $r(d+k)+k$. In PEFT’s transposed linear-layer layout, $k$ is the number of output rows. Table 1 gives 0.83% versus 0.84% trainable parameters on LLaMA-7B. The eight datasets are BoolQ, PIQA, SocialIQA, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge and OpenBookQA. The LoRA row comes from the baseline cited by the authors. Appendix A.2 measures a separate implementation ablation within DoRA at batch size 16 with four gradient accumulation steps. Detaching the norm reduced reported GPU memory from 37.3 GB to 28.2 GB on LLaMA-7B. At inference, compute the complete DoRA expression once and store it as the layer weight.
:::

## Conclusions · LoRA and scaling {#H11 .lora-slide .lora-conclusion}

::::: {.lora-body .conclusion-body}
:::: {.conclusion-spread}
::: {.conclusion-argument}
**The starting weights determine which factor can move first.**

With random $A$ and zero $B$, the first loss gradient can move $B$. With the same initialization and SGD rate, doubling the scale makes the first weight step **four times larger**.
:::

::: {.conclusion-detail data-lora-fit="true"}
**How much does tuning the two rates buy?**

| Llama-7B setup | Gain over equal rates |
|:--|--:|
| MMLU after Flan-v2 tuning · $r=64$ | **+1.3 pp** |
| MNLI · $r=8$, tested $\eta_B \ge \eta_A$ | **+0.1 pp** |

The two experiments had different ranks and tasks.
:::
::::
:::::

::: {.lora-takeaway}
When comparing ranks, record the initialization and scale, and tune the learning rate for each candidate.
:::

::: {.lora-source}
[Hu et al. · §4.1](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09685v2#page=4) · [Kalajdzievski · §3](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2312.03732v1#page=4) · [Hayou et al. · Fig. 5](https://arxiv.org/html/2402.12354v2#S5.F5)
:::

::: {.notes lang="en"}
In ordinary LoRA, $r$ bounds the rank of $\Delta W=sBA$. In DoRA this bound applies to the directional correction. The factorization also changes optimization. For the standard initialization, the loss gradient in $A$ vanishes and the gradient in $B$ can be nonzero. Under plain SGD, the first effective weight step contains the square of the branch multiplier. The LoRA+ comparisons are 44.0% versus 42.7% and 90.2% versus 90.1% in their respective grids. They motivate tuning the two rates without selecting a universal ratio. Next, keep the parameter budget fixed and change which weights receive it.
:::
